AUS.story:
Most of Australia's record is sexual abuse of children in institutions run by churches and the state. The Royal Commission into Institutional Responses to Child Sexual Abuse, which reported in 2017, heard evidence about 3,489 institutions; of survivors in its private sessions, 58.1% were abused in a religious institution and 32.5% in a government-run one. In the Catholic Church, 4,444 people reported abuse between 1980 and 2015, naming 1,880 alleged perpetrators, and 22% of Christian Brothers had been accused. Government bodies are also in the record. Senior navy staff knew of and tolerated widespread abuse of child recruits at the HMAS Leeuwin base until 1972, and in 2024 a Victorian inquiry found the education department had covered up abuse by teachers of more than 100 pupils.

Institutions kept offenders working by moving them without telling police. Bishop Ronald Mulkearns of Ballarat knew by late 1975 that the priest Gerald Ridsdale was abusing children and kept reappointing him; Ridsdale was later convicted of abusing more than 70 children. A police officer accepted the bishop's promise to deal with it, and in 1972 a senior officer offered a detective a promotion to stop investigating a monsignor. Julian Fox, a Salesian priest, was moved to Fiji in 1999 after police began investigating him. In 2008 the Adass Israel School in Melbourne flew its head teacher, Malka Leifer, to Israel before police were told; after an Israeli deputy minister interfered with her psychiatric assessments, she was extradited only in 2021, and she was convicted in 2023.

Governments also removed children from their families. A 1997 national inquiry, Bringing Them Home, examined the removal of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander children, known as the Stolen Generations. About 4,000 children were sent from Britain to Australian institutions from 1945 to 1970, and the inquiry for England and Wales found a catalogue of evidence of their sexual abuse.

Australians are also buyers abroad. A 2020 study ranked them third among people paying for livestreamed abuse of children in the Philippines, and the bank Westpac agreed a A$1.3 billion penalty that year that included failing to check such payments. About 800 registered child sex offenders travelled abroad in 2016, 40% without telling police; laws from 2017 allow their passports to be cancelled.

Between 2015 and 2018 every state and territory removed or changed the time limits on civil claims for child abuse, and a National Redress Scheme began in 2018. The Royal Commission referred 309 cases to police; the record does not say how many led to charges.

BHR.story:
The research for this map found no documented case of child sexual abuse or child trafficking in Bahrain, no recorded movement of children into or out of the country, and no organisation that recurs there. What exists are outside measures of trafficking and online abuse in general.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scored Bahrain's human trafficking market at 8 on a scale from 1 (none) to 10 (pervasive) in 2025. It scored the presence of criminals inside the state at 4.5 out of 10 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 5.33. The US State Department's 2025 Trafficking in Persons report placed Bahrain in Tier 1, its highest grade for a government's efforts. Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimated in 2023 that 11,000 people in Bahrain were in modern slavery, or 6.7 per 1,000; that figure covers adults as well as children, and all forms of forced labour and exploitation. In 2024 the US CyberTipline, run by the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children (NCMEC), received 10,637 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Bahrain, or 669.6 per 100,000 people.

Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates, found in its 2026 update that the Middle East and North Africa has no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children. How many children in Bahrain are abused or trafficked is not known.
===

CHE.story:
The largest part of Switzerland's record is the removal of children from their families by the authorities themselves. Cantonal and municipal authorities, without any court order, interned more than 60,000 people in about 650 institutions, mainly between 1930 and 1981, and placed children with farmers as indentured labourers, known as Verdingkinder. An independent expert commission set up by federal law reported in September 2019 that the people interned were abused physically, psychologically and sexually. A programme of the foundation Pro Juventute, backed by federal authorities, removed about 590 children of the Yenish, a travelling minority, from their families; in February 2025 the Swiss government recognised it as a crime against humanity.

Abuse also took place in Catholic institutions. A pilot study by historians at the University of Zurich, commissioned by the Swiss Bishops' Conference and religious orders and published in September 2023, documented 1,002 cases of sexual abuse in the Swiss Catholic Church since the mid-20th century, with 510 accused people and 921 victims; 74% of the documents concerned minors. More than half the cases took place in pastoral work and about 30% in Catholic children's homes, schools and boarding schools. The researchers found that church criminal law was hardly ever applied and that many cases were kept secret, covered up or played down, and called the cases "the tip of the iceberg".

Switzerland also received children from abroad through adoption. It took in 1,111 South Korean children between 1968 and 1997. Swiss authorities came to know that placements of children from countries such as Sri Lanka, India and Tibet were driven by money and linked to organised child trafficking, that children were often wrongly presented as orphans, and that decisions rested on incomplete or falsified documents. The Federal Council, the Swiss government, acknowledged the authorities' failures in 2020 and 2023 and recommended a general ban on intercountry adoption at the end of 2024.

Swiss men have also abused children abroad. A Swiss man from Lucerne, convicted of abusing children in Fribourg in 1980 and in Valais in 1991, returned to Thailand in 1996 and abused more than 80 boys in Pattaya and the north, mainly between 2002 and 2013. He also forced boys into acts with European clients at his bar, and a Swiss court sentenced him to 16 years in 2018.

The government apologised in 2010, and a 2016 law gives victims of the compulsory measures a "solidarity contribution" of CHF 25,000. The Church study's authors expect more cases than the 1,002 they found, and the record does not say whether the proposed adoption ban has become law.

CPV.story:
The research for this map found no documented case of child sexual abuse or child trafficking in Cape Verde, and no recorded movement of children into or out of the country.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC), a research network, scored Cape Verde's human trafficking market at 4.5 on a scale from 1 (none) to 10 (pervasive) in 2025, the presence of criminals inside the state at 4, and the country's resilience to organised crime at 6.54 out of 10. The US State Department's 2025 Trafficking in Persons report placed it on the Tier 2 Watch List, a grade for governments making efforts that it judges insufficient. These measures cover trafficking of all kinds and do not separate children.

Childlight, a research centre that combines surveys into global estimates, found in its 2026 update that West and Central Africa has no representative survey data on online sexual exploitation of children. The scale of abuse of children in Cape Verde is not known.
===

ECU.story:
The largest part of Ecuador's record is sexual violence against pupils by teachers and staff in public and private schools. It became a national issue after families of pupils at the Academia Aeronáutica Mayor Pedro Traversari (AAMPETRA), a school in Quito where 41 children were abused, organised and pressed the National Assembly, Ecuador's parliament. The Assembly set up a multiparty commission in 2017 to review cases from 2013 to 2017. Its report, approved unanimously on 16 February 2018, found negligence by public institutions, the Ministry of Education and judicial authorities, and concluded that former education ministers had not acted. Human Rights Watch, analysing government data, counted 4,221 pupils who suffered sexual violence in schools between 2014 and May 2020.

Abuse by Catholic clergy is the second documented form. A months-long investigation by Visión 360, a programme on the TV channel Ecuavisa, counted 103 complaints of sexual abuse involving Ecuadorian clergy in the provinces of Guayas, Pichincha, Azuay and Los Ríos, among them complaints concerning Fr César Cordero and Fr Luis Intriago. Victims' families said the church hierarchy refused to share information and did not take complaints to prosecutors itself. A survivors' association has demanded that these crimes be made imprescriptible, meaning they could be prosecuted however much time has passed, as approved in a referendum.

Ecuador is also linked in the map's records to a Norwegian government inquiry, published in June 2026, into adoptions from 12 countries since the 1950s. It found illegal or unethical practices, including falsified documents and payments to orphanages tied to the number of children adopted; the record does not say which findings concern children from Ecuador.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored criminals inside the Ecuadorian state at 7.5 out of 10 in 2025 and the human trafficking market at 6.5. Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimated 135,000 people in modern slavery in 2023, adults and children together. The US CyberTipline received 141,134 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Ecuador in 2024, or 778.2 per 100,000 people.

The 2018 commission named the failures of the education ministry and the courts, and pupils went on reporting sexual violence in schools through at least May 2020. The church has published no figures of its own in the record.

GAB.story:
Gabon's record is about Gabonese soldiers accused of sexually abusing children abroad, while serving as UN peacekeepers in the Central African Republic. The UN mission there is called MINUSCA. In 2016 it recorded two allegations about incidents in the town of Dékoa involving soldiers from Gabon and Burundi. Investigators interviewed some 136 alleged victims, who made up 48% of all victims recorded that year, according to the UN Secretary-General's 2017 report. Press accounts reported that at least 98 girls described abuse and that 41 soldiers were identified and sent home without charges.

Under UN rules, only the country that sends troops can prosecute them; the UN itself can only send them home. The 2017 report said the investigations by Gabon and Burundi were still pending, and the map's records list the soldiers as not charged. Allegations against the Gabonese contingent continued. In September 2021 the UN announced that all Gabonese military units in MINUSCA, about 450 personnel, would be sent home after allegations of sexual exploitation and abuse, and Gabon opened an investigation. The Secretary-General's 2022 report linked most of MINUSCA's 2021 allegations with more than one victim to a single troop-contributing country sent home that September.

The research found no documented case of child abuse or trafficking inside Gabon itself. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored criminals inside the Gabonese state at 7.5 out of 10 in 2025 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.5. Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimated 17,000 people in modern slavery in Gabon in 2023, adults and children together. Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online abuse of children for West and Central Africa.

No Gabonese soldier is recorded as charged for the abuse in the Central African Republic, and the result of Gabon's 2021 investigation is not in the record.

GRC.story:
Greece's record has two main parts: the adoption of Greek-born children abroad from 1950 to 1975, and the exposure of migrant children to trafficking today.

From 1950 to 1975 Greek-born children were sent for adoption to the United States, the Netherlands and Sweden. On 2 May 2025 Greece passed a law restoring Greek citizenship to about 4,000 of them. In Sweden, one of the receiving countries, a state inquiry reported in June 2025 on 65 years of intercountry adoption and documented numerous irregularities and illegal acts of which state authorities had some knowledge; the record does not say what it found about children from Greece.

The second part concerns children who arrive in Greece without their families. The US State Department's 2025 report says unaccompanied children in Greece are vulnerable to sex trafficking, and that Roma children from Albania, Bulgaria and Romania are forced to beg. In January 2016 Europol, the EU police agency, said at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, with evidence that some had been sexually exploited, and that a criminal infrastructure had grown up over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow. Europol's figures named Italy and Sweden; the record gives no number for Greece.

Greece also appears in international cases of online abuse. On 29 April 2025 the US Department of Justice announced the arrest in Greece of an alleged leader of "764 Inferno", a subgroup of 764, an online network that extorted minors into producing abuse material and harming themselves. It is listed among the countries involved in Project Spade, the 2013 Canadian case against the film distributor Azov Films, and in Operation Stream against the Kidflix site in 2025.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored criminals inside the Greek state at 7.5 out of 10 in 2025 and the human trafficking market at 5.5. Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimated 66,000 people in modern slavery in 2023, adults and children together.

The 2025 law addressed the citizenship of children adopted abroad, and the record holds no Greek inquiry into how those adoptions were arranged. The number of migrant children trafficked in Greece is not counted.

HUN.story:
The best-known Hungarian case is about how the state treated a cover-up in a children's home. In 2022 a court sentenced Endre Kónya, former deputy director of the children's home at Bicske, to three years and four months for helping the home's director cover up his sexual abuse of children. In April 2023, ahead of a visit by the Pope, President Katalin Novák pardoned about two dozen people, Kónya among them. The then justice minister, Judit Varga, countersigned the pardon. It became public in early February 2024, when the news site Telex reported it. After protests, Novák resigned on 10 February 2024, saying she had made a mistake, and Varga announced the same day that she was leaving public life. Prime Minister Orbán proposed a constitutional amendment barring pardons for crimes against children.

Hungary is also a country that sends children abroad for adoption. Figures compiled by the researcher Selman count 2,868 Hungarian children adopted abroad between 2003 and 2022, and the country has not closed or suspended the practice.

Hungary is named in Europol's account of migrant children who went missing in Europe. In January 2016 Europol, the EU police agency, said at least 10,000 unaccompanied children had disappeared after arriving in Europe, that it had evidence some had been sexually exploited, and that a criminal infrastructure had grown up over 18 months around exploiting the migrant flow, with many arrests in Germany and Hungary.

Suspects in Hungary appear in several international police operations against online abuse. In an operation led by New Zealand's Department of Internal Affairs from 2019, suspects in Hungary and Austria were found abusing their own children. People in Hungary were among those arrested over a private Skype group in 2018, and Hungary is listed among the countries involved in 2025 actions against the paid site Kidflix and a platform for AI-generated abuse material. The US CyberTipline received 21,136 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Hungary in 2024.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored criminals inside the Hungarian state at 7.5 out of 10 in 2025 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 4.79.

The pardon cost the president and a former minister their positions. The record holds no national inquiry into abuse in Hungarian children's homes.

ITA.story:
Italy has no independent national inquiry into abuse in institutions, so the only national figures on abuse by Catholic clergy come from the Italian Bishops' Conference (CEI) itself. Its first report, in November 2022, said dioceses had sent 613 files on clerics to the Vatican since 2000. Its 2025 report counted 115 alleged victims and 67 alleged perpetrators in 2023–2024. The victims' group Rete l'Abuso says the reports leave out court and Vatican cases. In May 2012 the CEI said that under the Lateran concordat, the treaty between Italy and the Holy See, its priests have no obligation to report suspected abuse to the police. The one fully independent study, of the Diocese of Bolzano-Bressanone in 2025, found 29 clerics responsible in 67 cases with 59 victims and called the diocese's handling of cases until 2010 a highly systemic failure.

Accused priests have moved across borders. Fr Nicola Corradi, accused at the Provolo school for deaf children in Verona in 2009, went on working at the order's school in Mendoza, Argentina, where a court sentenced him in 2019 to 42 years for abusing deaf children. Joseph Henn, a priest indicted in Arizona in 2003, lived in Italy and avoided a confirmed extradition until his arrest in Rome in 2019.

Juvenile courts and social services sent children for decades to Il Forteto, a farming community near Florence, although its founder, Rodolfo Fiesoli, had a final conviction from 1985. He was later definitively sentenced to 14 years and 10 months for abuse. A parliamentary commission set up in 2024 is examining why the authorities kept accrediting the community.

Italy is a destination for trafficked girls. In 2017 the International Organization for Migration said up to 80% of Nigerian women and girls arriving by sea could be trafficking victims, most aged 13 to 24. Nigerian groups control them through debt and rituals, and Eastern European girls are recruited online for sex trafficking in Italy. In 2016 Europol said 5,000 unaccompanied migrant children had disappeared in Italy.

Italians are also among the buyers abroad. A 2006 study by UNICEF and Kenya's government found Italian, German and Swiss tourists were 44% of the clients of exploited children on the Kenyan coast. Italy has also adopted children from countries where inquiries later found fraud or army involvement, among them 383 from South Korea and others from wartime Guatemala and El Salvador.

The Forteto commission is still working, and the clergy figures remain the Church's own.

KHM.story:
The largest part of Cambodia's record is the sale of children for sex, to foreign men and Cambodian men, in brothels and tourist areas. Its best-documented centre was Svay Pak, a poor fishing village near Phnom Penh, where most of the children were ethnic Vietnamese sold by destitute families. Observers reported in 2002 that it grew with Western sex tourism after Thailand cracked down on child prostitution.

Local officials protected the brothels. The police raid on Svay Pak on 22 January 2003 was widely advertised in advance; almost all the children had been moved to Siem Reap and Sihanoukville, and no pimps or clients were arrested. Local authorities had been extorting brothel owners. After the government shut the Svay Pak brothels in 2005, the trade moved to less visible places such as massage parlours and karaoke bars. Survey estimates of the share of minors among sex workers fell from nearly 35% to 1–2% by 2017, but CNN reported that year that families in Svay Pak were still selling girls. The US State Department's 2025 report says men from Cambodia, Australia, South Africa, the United States and elsewhere exploit children in tourism, increasingly through social media, that children as young as 13 are held in brothels to pay family debts, and that official complicity at senior levels hinders enforcement.

In 2009 Cambodian police arrested three previously convicted US sex offenders who had travelled repeatedly to buy children, and the US charged them in Los Angeles; the head of US Immigration and Customs Enforcement called Cambodia "ground zero for child sex tourism".

Children were also bought for adoption and for orphanages. The US facilitator Lauryn Galindo arranged about 800 adoptions to American families between 1997 and 2001, more than half of all Cambodian adoptions; the US government said her business paid Cambodian mothers for babies. The US suspended adoptions in late 2001, and in 2004 Galindo pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit visa fraud and money laundering, admitting she falsified documents. The State Department reported in 2019 that some orphanages buy children from poor families to attract donations. In 2017 Australia's parliament, whose citizens fund and volunteer at such orphanages, classed orphanage trafficking as modern slavery.

The State Department rates Cambodia Tier 3, its lowest grade, and the research network Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime scored criminals inside the state at 9 out of 10 in 2025. Open street sale in Svay Pak has ended, and exploitation in hidden venues, through social media and in scam compounds continues.

LVA.story:
Latvia's record centres on one child exploitation ring in Riga that came to light in 1999, and on the political accusations that followed it. After a Latvian TV report in September 1999, prosecutors investigated Logos Centrs, a video and model agency in Riga headed by Jurijs Jurjevs. The newspaper The Baltic Times described it as a bogus modelling agency running a child pornography and prostitution ring. According to Wikipedia, citing Latvian media, the agency had catalogued about 3,000 minors, and 67 people, 61 of them minors, were sexually exploited.

The courts convicted customers as well as organisers. Seven people were charged. Andris Meinarts was convicted on 21 counts of sexually abusing minors as a customer and received ten years, the maximum sentence. Ainārs Eisaks, a pageant agency manager, received two and a half years. By the Wikipedia account, Jurjevs received more than four years and Ingus Tūns, tried separately, five.

Claims that powerful men were among the clients were investigated and found false. The Saeima, Latvia's parliament, set up an investigation commission chaired by the opposition MP Jānis Ādamsons. On 17 February 2000 he publicly linked the former prime minister Andris Šķēle, the former justice minister Valdis Birkavs and the head of the State Revenue Service, Andrejs Sončiks, to the case. On 1 August 2000 the Prosecutor General's Office closed the cases against them, stating it was "fully proved" that the information given to the commission about them was false. None of them was charged. Ādamsons was later convicted of slander, and in February 2007 the Supreme Court upheld a fine of 10,400 lats.

Latvia has also been a country that sent children abroad for adoption. A Latvian law preventing adoptions to the United States took effect on 1 July 2022, according to a US government report. Latvia is listed among the countries involved in two international investigations of paid online abuse sites, Regpay in 2003 and Kidflix in 2025; the record does not say what part Latvia played in either.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored Latvia's resilience to organised crime at 7.63 out of 10 in 2025 and criminals inside the state at 2.5.

The Logos Centrs case ended in convictions, and the accusations against senior officials were disproved. The record holds no national inquiry into abuse in Latvian institutions.

MLT.story:
Malta's record has two parts: abuse of minors by priests inside Malta, counted by the Catholic Church itself, and abuse of Maltese children sent to institutions in Australia under child migration schemes.

The only national figures on clergy abuse come from the Church. In 1991 the Maltese bishops set up a Response Team, chaired by Judge Victor Caruana Colombo, to deal with complaints. In April 2010 the Curia, the Church's central office in Malta, said the team had handled 45 cases of abuse of minors by priests over 19 years. Nineteen were dismissed as unfounded, 13 were still open, four priests were found guilty and removed from ministry, and two priests had died. Separate criminal convictions concern St Joseph Home. The record holds no state inquiry into abuse in Maltese institutions.

The second part took place abroad. Children from Malta and Britain were sent to Australia as child migrants. Among the institutions that received them were those of the Christian Brothers, a Catholic teaching order, at Bindoon, Castledare, Clontarf and Tardun in Western Australia. In 2001 an Australian Senate committee report, "Lost Innocents", found that 38 of the 207 former child migrants who made submissions described sexual abuse, 24 of them in Christian Brothers institutions in Western Australia. The committee described "systemic criminal sexual assault" by a large number of Brothers over a long period. Australia's Royal Commission, a national inquiry, was told in 2017 that 22% of Christian Brothers in Australia between 1950 and 2010 had been the subject of child sexual abuse allegations, and that the order's leaders knew of abuse at the Western Australian orphanages for decades. The record does not say how many of the abused child migrants were Maltese.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored state-embedded criminal actors at 7.5 out of 10 in 2025. Malta is also listed among the countries involved in Operation Stream, the 2025 international action against the paid abuse streaming site Kidflix.

Abuse of the child migrants has been documented by Australian inquiries. Inside Malta, the counts available are the Church's own.

NGA.story:
The largest part of Nigeria's record is the trafficking of women and girls for sex abroad, mostly from Edo State; the UN Office on Drugs and Crime is cited as finding that at least nine in ten Nigerian women trafficked to Europe come from there. Women and girls are moved overland through Niger and Libya and by boat to Italy, bound by debt and by oaths sworn before traditional priests. In 2017 the International Organization for Migration said up to 80% of Nigerian women and girls arriving in Italy by sea could be trafficking victims, most aged 13 to 24. Female arrivals rose from 1,500 in 2014 to more than 11,000 in 2016. Organised groups, some linked to Nigerian confraternities (secret fraternal societies), run the trade in Italy, Spain and Britain; a Palermo court convicted 14 members of a Black Axe cell in 2018. Other networks take girls to gold mines elsewhere in West Africa, including Senegal. In March 2018 Edo's traditional ruler, the Oba of Benin, Ewuare II, revoked the oaths, and anecdotal evidence suggested trafficking slowed. The US State Department's 2025 report counts 49 traffickers convicted in a year and names official complicity, including among anti-trafficking officials, as a significant concern.

In the north-east, the armed groups Boko Haram (JAS) and ISWAP abduct children, many of them from schools. Boko Haram abducted 276 girls at Chibok in 2014; 82 were still captive in April 2024, and 20 released girls had been forced to marry former fighters. ISWAP took 110 girls from Dapchi in 2018. In 2024 the UN verified 991 abductions of children in Nigeria, 637 of them girls, and sexual violence, all through forced marriage, against 419 children.

"Baby factories" are places posing as clinics, maternity homes or orphanages where pregnant girls are held and their babies sold, including for adoption. Police raided them in Enugu in 2008, in Aba in 2011, freeing 32 pregnant girls mostly aged 15 to 17, and in Lagos in 2018, rescuing 162 children, some sexually abused. Nigeria still sends children abroad for adoption: 3,263 between 2003 and 2022 by the researcher Selman's count.

Nigeria-based offenders also extort teenagers abroad. Two brothers in Lagos, Samuel and Samson Ogoshi, posed as a girl online to obtain explicit images from a 17-year-old in Michigan, who died by suicide; extradited to the US, they were sentenced in 2024 to 17.5 years each.

The 2024 and 2025 UN and US reports describe abductions and trafficking as continuing. The record lists raids on baby factories; their total number is not known.

PAN.story:
The main documented form of abuse in Panama is in shelters for children at social risk. The shelters, called albergues, are run by private bodies and non-governmental organisations under the supervision of the Secretaría de Niñez, Adolescencia y Familia (Senniaf), the state agency for children and families. In early February 2021 a subcommission of the National Assembly, Panama's parliament, reported cases of abuse in the shelters. By March 2021 the Public Ministry, the prosecution service, had opened 18 criminal investigations, inspected 57 shelters, interviewed about 280 children and identified 20 victims, who were moved; five people had been charged with offences including child mistreatment, embezzlement and sexual offences. The Ombudsman found irregularities in 34% of 52 shelters inspected and found that 70% of 44 lacked suitable staff and that Senniaf did little follow-up.

Abuse has also been found in the homes of an international children's charity. An independent commission appointed by SOS Children's Villages, which runs children's homes in many countries, named Panama in its 2023 report. It confirmed serious allegations of sexual and physical abuse in several member associations in Africa, Asia and Central America, and found that former senior staff in more than one association covered up abuse and did not report it to national authorities.

Panama also figures in online and cross-border exploitation. In 2025 the Internet Watch Foundation, a British charity that removes abuse images, took action against 5,275 web addresses hosted in Panama, 2% of its total. In October 2024 police arrested a man in Puerto Caimito, La Chorrera, accused of contacting minors through the gaming platform Roblox and threatening them to obtain abuse images; the alert came from Spanish police. A sex network run from Cartagena, Colombia, by Liliana del Carmen Campos Puello, who was convicted of human trafficking in 2018, sent young women to Panama, Mexico, Miami and the Bahamas.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored Panama's human trafficking market at 7 out of 10 in 2025 and criminals inside the state at 7.5. Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimated 20,000 people in modern slavery in 2023, adults and children together.

The 2021 inquiries led to five people being charged and 20 children being moved. The record does not say how the cases ended or whether Senniaf's supervision of the shelters changed.

PRY.story:
The largest form of child exploitation on Paraguay's record today is criadazgo, the practice of families taking in children to work for them as unpaid domestic servants. The US State Department's 2025 report calls it a common form of trafficking in Paraguay and estimates that 47,000 children live in criadazgo, most of them girls; boys are 30 percent. The report says many of them are highly vulnerable to sex and labour trafficking.

Under the Stroessner dictatorship from 1954 to 1989, the state itself abused girls. Paraguay's Truth and Justice Commission, created by law in 2003, in its final report of 28 August 2008 found that the repressive apparatus fostered sexual violence against women and girls, which reached its extreme in "sexual slavery of girls practised by senior officers of the regime". Procurers took girls from their families for the officers, and young children were exploited economically and sexually in military posts at the service of officers. The commission recorded that 10.8% of victims were minors and noted large under-reporting of sexual violence. Amnesty International reported that girls as young as seven were believed to have been taken from their homes for senior officers.

Paraguay has also received Catholic priests accused of abuse elsewhere. The Argentine priest Carlos Urrutigoity, accused in the US in 2002 of abuse involving students and a seminarian in the Diocese of Scranton, moved with his group to Ciudad del Este, where Bishop Rogelio Livieres made him vicar general, the bishop's deputy, in 2014. Pope Francis removed Livieres that year, reportedly in part over the case, and Urrutigoity was moved to Mendoza, Argentina, in 2015. He has not been convicted. The newspaper La Nación reported that at least five Argentine priests accused of abuse or of crimes against humanity had sheltered in Paraguay. One of the German administrators of Boystown, a darknet abuse platform with about 400,000 users, was living in Paraguay and arrested there in 2021.

Paraguay sent children abroad for adoption in the 1990s. The US issued 1,142 immigrant visas to children adopted from Asunción in the fiscal years 1994 to 2003, 483 of them in 1994.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored criminals inside the state at 9 out of 10 in 2025 and the country's resilience to organised crime at 3.29.

Criadazgo continues on the scale the 2025 report estimates. The Truth Commission documented the regime's abuse of girls, and the record does not show any officer convicted for it.

SEN.story:
The largest part of Senegal's record is the forced begging of talibé children, pupils who live and study at residential Quranic schools called daaras. Human Rights Watch and the Senegalese rights platform PPDH reported in June 2019 that more than 100,000 talibés are forced by some of their teachers, called marabouts, to beg every day, often under quotas enforced by beatings. The children live under the teachers' control, and the abuse recorded at the schools goes beyond begging. For 2017 and 2018 the two groups documented 16 deaths of talibés from beatings, neglect or endangerment, 61 cases of beatings, 15 cases of rape, attempted rape or sexual abuse and 14 of children chained or imprisoned, in 8 of Senegal's 14 regions. The US State Department's 2025 report says the government identified 573 child victims of forced begging in a year.

The second form is sex trafficking of girls at gold-mining sites. In the south-eastern mining region of Kédougou, traffickers exploit women and girls as young as 12, according to the State Department's 2025 report. Senegal is a destination for this trafficking. Most victims come from Nigeria, where organised networks, some linked to cult groups, move women and girls to mining regions in Senegal, Mali, Burkina Faso and Côte d'Ivoire. Others come from Senegal itself, Mali, Benin, Burkina Faso, Ghana, Guinea, Sierra Leone and China. The same report says some tourists exploit children in Dakar and Saint-Louis, and to a lesser extent in Cap Skirring and La Petite Côte.

A third, smaller record concerns foreign missionaries. New Tribes Mission, a US-based evangelical mission now called Ethnos360, ran a boarding school at Fanda for missionaries' children. A 2010 report by GRACE, a Christian group that investigates abuse, which the mission commissioned after pressure from survivors, accused it of systemic abuse there, including sexual abuse of more than 20 children. Notes from a 1992 meeting of the mission's field committee said allegations should not be reported to the police.

Childlight, a research centre, found no representative survey data on online abuse of children for West and Central Africa.

The 2019 count of more than 100,000 children forced to beg is the latest in the record, and the 2025 report still describes girls trafficked to the Kédougou mines. Their number is not counted.

SVN.story:
Slovenia's documented record of abuse of children in an institution is a single Catholic priest who left the country to avoid prosecution. Fr Franc Frantar, a priest of the Archdiocese of Ljubljana, abused up to 16 minors. He first avoided prosecution by going to Malawi as a missionary, and returned to Slovenia only after Interpol, the international police organisation, issued a notice for him. He was detained in 2006 and later sentenced; sources give three and a half or five years. The record does not say whether church authorities knew of the abuse before he left.

The map's records also link Slovenia to Nazi Germany's taking of children during the Second World War. The SS Race and Settlement Main Office (RuSHA) and the Lebensborn organisation selected children judged "racially valuable" in occupied territories and placed them with German families under new identities. In 1948 a US military tribunal at Nuremberg convicted 13 of the 14 officials tried for this, among other crimes. The record gives no figure for children taken from Slovenia.

The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored Slovenia's human trafficking market at 4.5 out of 10 in 2025 and criminals inside the state at 6.5. The US State Department placed Slovenia in Tier 1, its highest grade. Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimated 9,000 people in modern slavery in 2023, adults and children together, and the US CyberTipline received 4,110 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in Slovenia in 2024.

The record holds no national inquiry into abuse in Slovenian institutions, so the extent of abuse beyond the Frantar case is not known.

TTO.story:
The documented record of institutional abuse in Trinidad and Tobago comes from its children's homes. In 1997 the Cabinet appointed a task force, chaired by Robert Sabga, which visited nine homes. It found that a male employee at St Dominic's Children's Home had repeatedly sexually abused some 30 to 40 children. When the abuse was discovered, he was asked to resign, and he was allegedly helped to find work at a hospital. The task force also recorded beatings at St Jude's School for Girls.

The government did not publish the report. Its findings became public only in May 2022, when the newspaper Trinidad Express published them, 25 years after the task force reported. The record shows no prosecution arising from it.

The second documented form is sex trafficking into the country. The US State Department's 2025 Trafficking in Persons report says the victims are mainly women and girls from Venezuela, Colombia, the Dominican Republic and Guyana, and that non-governmental organisations allege officials help with their transport and entry. The Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime, a research network, scored the human trafficking market at 6.5 out of 10 in 2025 and criminals inside the state at 5. Walk Free, an anti-slavery group, estimated 7,000 people in modern slavery in 2023, adults and children together. The US CyberTipline received 7,853 reports of suspected online child sexual abuse located in the country in 2024, or 573.9 per 100,000 people.

The Sabga findings have been public since 2022. The record does not say what happened to the St Dominic's employee. How many of the trafficked women and girls are children is not counted.

USA.story:
Most of the US record is abuse of children in churches, sports bodies, universities, youth organisations and state care. There has been no national inquiry; investigations have been run by state attorneys general, grand juries and church-commissioned studies. In the cases on record, complaints reached someone in authority years before anyone acted. Athletes complained about the gymnastics team doctor Larry Nassar from 1997; USA Gymnastics and then the FBI were told in 2015, the FBI did not act, and the Justice Department's inspector general found at least 70 more athletes were abused before his arrest in 2016. At Penn State, a 1998 police report on Jerry Sandusky was not prosecuted, and university leaders did not take a 2001 eyewitness report to police. The Boy Scouts of America kept internal files on suspected abusers.

Institutions facing these claims have used bankruptcy and lobbying. At least 41 Catholic dioceses and orders, the Boy Scouts and USA Gymnastics filed for bankruptcy, and Catholic, insurance and Scout groups lobbied in several states against extending the legal deadlines for suing.

Wealth and status also shaped prosecutions. Palm Beach police identified about 35 girls in their investigation of the financier Jeffrey Epstein, and a state grand jury returned a single count of soliciting prostitution in 2006. In 2007 the US Attorney's office for southern Florida, under Alexander Acosta, agreed not to prosecute him or several suspected co-conspirators and kept the deal from the victims; he served 13 months. Federal sex-trafficking charges came only in 2019, and he died in custody that year. Ghislaine Maxwell was convicted in 2021 of sex trafficking of a minor and sentenced to 20 years.

The government itself ran institutions where children were abused. The Interior Department documented 417 federal Indian boarding schools from 1819 to 1969, with at least 973 child deaths and physical, sexual and emotional abuse.

The US has received adopted children on a large scale, including 109,242 from South Korea between 1953 and 2008 and 87,704 from China between 1994 and 2014. Americans ran some of the fraudulent schemes. Lauryn Galindo in Cambodia and Paul Petersen, an elected Arizona official who paid Marshallese women to give up their babies, both pleaded guilty. The 2003 PROTECT Act lets the US prosecute citizens who abuse children abroad. Online, the US CyberTipline received 2,061,893 reports located in the country in 2024, and the US hosted 16% of the abuse web addresses the Internet Watch Foundation acted on in 2025.

Nassar and Maxwell were convicted and sentenced. The Boy Scouts alone faced more than 82,000 abuse claims in its 2020 bankruptcy, and no national count of victims exists.

ZAF.story:
The largest part of South Africa's record is sexual abuse of children by adults in schools. After a complaint about an educator at St John's College in Mthatha, the South African Human Rights Commission released a report on 29 June 2026 describing sexual violence in schools as systemic and entrenched. It recorded 826 complaints of sexual misconduct to the South African Council for Educators, the teachers' professional body, between 2021 and 2025. The Commission found gaps in the registers meant to keep offenders away from children. A teacher struck off by the Council is not automatically placed on the safeguarding register, and 10,748 convicted offenders had not yet been entered on the National Register for Sex Offenders.

The second form is trafficking of children inside the country and into it. The US State Department's 2025 report says traffickers recruit children from rural areas and exploit them for sex in the cities, especially in Gauteng and Western Cape; brothel owners use drugs to control them, and some parents exploit their own children in sex trafficking or online for money or drugs. Low-level official corruption and complicity persisted, the report says. Other State Department reports describe girls exploited along the highway from Maputo, in Mozambique, to South Africa, and migrants moved south from the Dzaleka camp in Malawi, some of whom end up in sex trafficking in South Africa. Children also leave through adoption: by the researcher Selman's count, 3,716 South African children were adopted abroad between 2003 and 2022.

South Africa has also received foreign abusers. Fettes College in Edinburgh dismissed the teacher Iain Wares in 1979 but gave him a glowing testimonial, and he later abused children while teaching in South Africa; South Africa approved his extradition to Scotland, which he was still contesting in 2025. Fr Georg Kerkhoff, a German priest with abuse cases pending at home, worked in South Africa for years, was tried there for abusing boys at a 2008 camp, and was extradited and jailed in Krefeld, Germany, in 2015. The English barrister John Smyth, who abused boys he met through evangelical camps in England and Zimbabwe and was never charged, moved to South Africa in 2001; a 2024 review found it highly likely he kept abusing until his death in Cape Town in 2018.

The record does not say whether the 10,748 offenders have since been registered. The 2025 report describes trafficking of rural children to the cities as continuing.
